title: India and the US Are 'Very, Very Close' to a Historic Trade Deal — but One Number Stands in the Way
excerpt: With USTR Jamieson Greer wrapping up talks in New Delhi and Trade Minister Goyal claiming the deal is nearly done, the only remaining obstacle is a politically explosive tariff gap with Pakistan that no Indian leader can accept.
body:
After months of stop-start negotiations, the India-US trade deal appears closer to reality than at any point since its February 2026 announcement — but a single political constraint threatens to derail the finish line.

'Very, Very Close'

US Deputy Assistant Secretary Bethany Poulos Morrison offered the most direct American assessment yet. "Looking at trade, in February 2026, we announced the intention to finally conclude the historic trade deal. We are very, very close," she said at a public event this week.

Her comments came as US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer wrapped up a two-day negotiating session in New Delhi with Indian Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal and Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman. Both sides described the talks as substantive and productive.

The broader framework — what both governments call the Bilateral Trade Agreement (BTA) — envisions an interim pact followed by a comprehensive agreement. The stated ambition is "Mission 500": $500 billion in bilateral trade by 2030, up from $149 billion in goods trade in 2025, which Morrison called "a historic year."

"This is going to open India's market of 1.4 billion to America's goods on terms that are reciprocal and mutually beneficial," she said.

The Pakistan Problem

But the deal's most stubborn obstacle isn't about market access or regulatory alignment. It's about a two-and-a-half-percentage-point tariff gap with Pakistan.

The current US tariff on Indian goods stands at 12.5 percent. Pakistan's rate: 10 percent. For New Delhi, this is a political non-starter.

> ""Looking at trade, in February 2026, we announced the intention to finally conclude the historic trade deal."

"No political leader in India will accept that because it would essentially cost them elections," said Mukesh Aghi, president and CEO of the US-India Strategic Partnership Forum (USISPF), speaking ahead of the USISPF Leadership Summit in Washington.

The original deal framework, negotiated when broad US reciprocal tariffs had pushed Indian duties to 50 percent, offered India an 18 percent rate — crucially lower than the rates imposed on ASEAN competitors like Vietnam and Bangladesh. That competitive edge was the entire basis of the deal's attractiveness to New Delhi.

Then the US Supreme Court invalidated Trump's sweeping tariff regime. The legal landscape shifted, and the 18 percent comparative advantage evaporated.

Goyal, speaking at the India Global Forum's UK-India Week in London, was blunt: "The whole deal was centred around that competitive advantage we got with that 18 per cent over our neighbours and competing countries. We were lower than all our neighbouring countries and all our ASEAN countries other than Singapore. That is why the deal was attractive for us."

He added a firm deadline of sorts: India wants the deal finalised before July 24, when Washington's temporary 10 percent tariff on trading partners expires. "The faster, the better."

What the Deal Would Mean for NRI Investors

A successful trade agreement would have concrete implications for the Indian diaspora, particularly the estimated 4.4 million Indian-Americans and millions more NRIs in the US, UK, and Canada.

For the Indian stock market, a deal would likely trigger a broad sentiment rally. Indian equities have already logged three straight weekly gains on the back of falling oil prices and the RBI's dovish stance. A trade agreement would remove one of the last major overhangs on foreign institutional investor flows, which have been tentative amid diplomatic tensions.

For Indian exporters, the stakes are enormous. Key sectors positioned to benefit include IT services, pharmaceuticals, textiles, and agricultural products. The textile sector alone saw stocks surge this week after Motilal Oswal initiated coverage projecting export-led growth — a trend that a trade deal would accelerate.

For NRI professionals, the deal's broader BTA framework includes provisions on investment promotion and economic security alignment. India has signalled interest in deeper cooperation on artificial intelligence, quantum computing, critical minerals, and space — all sectors where diaspora talent plays an outsized role.

For remittances and dollar deposits, the trade deal's potential to strengthen the rupee would directly affect the millions of NRIs who send money home or hold Foreign Currency Non-Resident (FCNR) deposits. The RBI recently sweetened these deposits, offering rates as high as 6–7 percent — but exchange-rate stability remains the key variable.

What's Still Uncertain

Beyond the tariff gap, several complications lurk. The US Trade Representative's Section 301 probe into alleged overcapacity and forced labour in India and other countries remains active and could generate new friction. India is also wary of Washington imposing new tariffs even after a deal is signed.

The diplomatic backdrop is strained. The death of three Indian sailors in US Navy attacks on commercial ships in the Gulf earlier this year added a layer of public anger that makes any perceived capitulation on trade terms politically toxic in India.

India's negotiators also want the deal to include safeguards against future unilateral tariff actions — essentially, a commitment that the rules won't change again.

The Timeline

Both sides appear to want a deal before the July 24 deadline. Greer's visit was the latest in a series of accelerating face-to-face rounds — Indian negotiators were in Washington in April, and Greer himself visited in late June.

Aghi was cautiously optimistic: "I think that's where the administration will huddle and see how to find a solution that is a win-win for both India and the US."

But until Washington finds a mechanism to give India a tariff rate lower than Pakistan's — whether through executive action, congressional carve-out, or creative legal interpretation — the deal's final signature remains just out of reach.

*Sources: Reuters; The Indian Eye; US-India Strategic Partnership Forum; India Global Forum*
